BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: As the shortwave in the short-term period departs, the main low will begin moving its way through our area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry through Thursday, with near normal temperatures.
- Precipitation chances increasing across higher terrain Friday afternoon. Becoming widespread Saturday afternoon.
- A drying and warming trend will set in Monday, through at least midweek.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Following the departing shortwave, a drying and clearing trend will continue this morning. These clearing skies will allow for good radiational cooling; which, when combined with the recent precipitation, will allow for the development of fog/freezing fog this morning (especially in sheltered valleys). Temperatures this afternoon will generally be in the 50s in the low elevations, and 40s in the Oregon high desert and higher Idaho Basins. As flow aloft backs to be out of the southwest, thanks to a deepening low off the west coast, a warming trend will set in Thursday afternoon (highs around 5 degrees warmer than today). Before this, clear overnight skies tonight allow for cooler low temps. The majority of lower elevations will reach near or below freezing Thursday morning, with lows of 10-20 degrees in the Oregon high desert and higher Idaho basins.

A weak shortwave rotating through this low will bring an increase of high cloud cover Thursday. Another consequence of this shortwave will be increasing precipitation chances early Friday over the central Idaho mountains. The southwesterly flow aloft will keep snow levels high and snow accumulations low, with a dusting to an inch of snow expected above 6kft.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: As the shortwave in the short-term period departs, the main low will begin moving its way through our area. This trough will have a good pull of Pacific moisture ahead of it, with precipitable water values increasing to around the 90th percentile in southwest Idaho. The better juxtaposition of forcing and moisture will fall over southwest Idaho, which will lead to increasing precipitation chances through the day Saturday, reaching 50-80% Saturday evening and night as a cold front crosses the area. That being said, an umbrella may be a fine addition to your Halloween costume. Snow levels will initially begin at 6-8 kft MSL, lowering to 4.5-6.5 kft MSL by Sunday afternoon. These lowering snow levels will coincide with decreasing precipitation chances as conditions dry out behind the front. Overall, the bulk of any snow accumulation will remain above 6.5 kft MSL, with generally 2-5 inches of accumulation (Locally up to 7 on the highest peaks). The lowering snow levels could allow for snow or wintry mix as low as 4.5 kft Sunday, although little accumulation is anticipated as precipitation tapers off behind the departing system. Ridging will build in behind the departing system, allowing for dry conditions Monday afternoon through at least mid- week. Temperatures will be seasonable or below normal throughout the period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A strong cold front is set to bring below average temperatures on Monday, with model guidance suggesting quite a bit of spread in solutions.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and mostly dry through the work week.

- Unsettled weather potentially returning late in the weekend and early next week. There are many scenarios for how the weather will turn out but snow in the mountains is the most likely impact from this system. One possibility results in the lower elevations seeing their first snowfall of the season.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Current observations show areas of fog over parts of the northeast CO plains. A Dense Fog Advisory is currently in effect for Sedgwick and Phillips counties, where visibilities have dropped below 1/2 mile. The Dense Fog Advisory may have to be extended later tonight as the fog continues to expand west, with patchy fog reaching as far west as Greeley. Subsidence and a patch of mid level clouds should limit fog potential over the Denver metro. We expect fog to diminish by mid morning due to daytime heating, with the South Platte River valley likely clearing last.

Cross-barrier (west-southwest) flow will make Wednesday quite a breezy day, particularly early in the day as mountain wave and downsloping enhancement occurs. Wind gusts up to 35 mph will be possible at the high elevations, with gusts up 55 mph possible above 12,000 ft MSL. Temperatures will run above average for the plains and Denver metro, with highs reaching the upper 60s and low 70s. If an opaque mountain wave cloud is able to persist into the afternoon, as was seen on Monday, temperatures could stay a couple of degrees cooler for areas directly under the cloud cover. Flow aloft weakens and turns southwesterly on Thursday. Winds should remain light due to the weakening pressure gradient, and this should be a sunny fall day with temperatures only slightly above normal for the time of year.

Moisture from the remnants of Tropical Storm Vance will be advected north into our region on Friday. However, the bulk of the moisture should remain well to our south and east, mainly over the Texas Panhandle and central Plains. We have kept some 15-30% PoPs over the easternmost counties of our CWA, where some light rain seems reasonable late Friday evening. For the rest of our area, an increase in high clouds may be all that transpires as a result of this first plume of moisture.

Moisture remains elevated on Saturday, with precipitable water (PW) values generally between the 75th and 90th percentile of climatology over much of the state. A shortwave trough should bring enough QG ascent for a few sprinkles (15-25% chance) over the eastern CO plains, and rain/snow showers over the mountains (30-50% chance) in the afternoon.

The synoptic pattern becomes more complex on Sunday as an upper level trough and a subtropical jet approach the Four Corners. The subtropical jet is set to channel impressive Pacific moisture to parts of Arizona and New Mexico, akin to an atmospheric river. At this time, the bulk of the moisture plume appears to stay well to our south once again. Southwest flow aloft may still bring anomalous moisture to north-central CO, although this regime would primarily favor downsloping, which is not ideal for meaningful precipitation over the mountains of our CWA or the Denver area. Nevertheless, cloud cover and at least some light rain seems increasingly likely for Sunday, with light snow above 10,000 ft MSL.

A strong cold front is set to bring below average temperatures on Monday, with model guidance suggesting quite a bit of spread in solutions. With lingering moisture over the area, some mountain snow accumulations are becoming increasingly likely during the day on Monday. While a few deterministic and ensemble members do hint at least some dustings or light snow accumulations over the Palmer Divide and parts of the Denver metro, ensemble means suggest temperatures that would not be supportive of snow (40s-50s). This will be a system to watch as snow levels are likely to reach the foothills.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: In lieu of that, we can discuss some possible scenarios. Approximately 45% of LREF members are clustered into a scenario showing a more progressive storm system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry, warm, and breezy conditions are expected to continue through Thursday, with mild overnight lows.
- Chances for a few showers return Friday into Saturday (Halloween) with temperatures remaining mild.
- A pattern change to colder, wetter, and windier conditions is favored Sunday into Tuesday, but the details remain highly uncertain at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Another relatively quiet night is in store for SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle, with no widespread precipitation expected aside from a few light showers that may manage to sneak into northern and western portions of Carbon County. These are associated with a weak mid-level disturbance that is currently moving across Western Wyoming and Utah which can be seen clearly on GOES mid-level water vapor imagery. Although most areas will remain dry, did decide to increase PoPs mainly for Rawlins and points north and west if a shower does decide to sneak into the area.

Current METARs and web cameras are showing some dense fog across Box Butte, Morrill, and Cheyenne Counties in the Nebraska Panhandle, so went ahead and included these areas in a Dense Fog Advisory until 8AM MDT. Will have to monitor trends via satellite imagery across the western counties of the Nebraska Panhandle for fog, however expecting the most widespread, dense fog to remain east of a Scottsbluff to Kimball line. The moist conditions this morning are being driven by a weak lee trough which is inducing SE cyclonic upslope flow, and is expected to cease into the day as the flow becomes more out of the west or southwest. As we know, westerly winds translates to downslope flow in our area, and therefore adiabatic warming as the air descends the higher terrain onto lower elevations, so we can expect a similarly mild day to Tuesday. High temperatures are expected to again stand 5-10 degrees above average for this time of year, with low to mid 60s forecast east of the I-25 corridor, and low to mid 50s east of the Laramie Range. As for our winds, not expecting as strong of winds as we did yesterday over the wind-prone areas along I-80, however cannot rule out some gusts of 50-55 mph around sunrise. 700 mb flow will begin to relax by noon as weak shortwave ridging builds across the Northern Rockies. Expect another quiet night overnight into Thursday underneath the weak ridge, with mostly clear skies and generally light winds.

Lows on Thursday morning are still expected to be fairly mild for this time of year, with locations in the Nebraska Panhandle staying mainly in the upper 30s to low 40s, with SE Wyoming staying above freezing in the low to mid 30s, although Laramie may briefly dip below freezing. For perspective, the average low in Cheyenne on Thursday is 30 degrees, with a low of 37 degrees currently in the forecast. During the day on Thursday, the mid-level ridge will begin to amplify over the Upper-Midwest, placing us in a SW flog regime. This will continue the trend of dry and warmer than average conditions as NAEFS guidance has 500 mb geopotential height values ranging from the 75-80th percentile underneath the building ridge. This will translate to high temperatures mainly in the low to mid- 60s east of the Laramie Range, and slightly cooler mid to upper 50s in places like Laramie and Rawlins. Another mild night is expected Thursday into Friday, with many locations in the Nebraska Panhandle struggling to dip below 40 degrees by Friday morning, and the population centers (at least for Wyoming standards) across SE Wyoming staying above freezing in the mid to upper 30s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A broad, upper-level ridge will sit across the central CONUS Friday morning leading to modest southwesterly flow across the region. Unlike previous patterns, this ridge will not be as strong and temperatures will not warm nearly as much. The next upper-level system will be slowly moving into the Pacific Northwest throughout much of the day Friday, though its progression will be slow. The base of the trough will remain offshore through at least early Saturday morning. A very weak shortwave will attempt to push through the region on Friday, leading to very weak, synoptic ascent mainly across western Nebraska and mainly later in the day as the shortwave approaches the region. 700mb slow remains from the southwest and fairly weak, with the shortwave barely visible as it progresses northeastward and is, ultimately, absorbed into the larger scale flow. 700mb temperatures remain in the 4 to 6C range across the region throughout the day Friday, so expect temperatures in the upper-50s to low-60s everywhere. Surface is currently forecast to be out of the south-southeast for all locations east of the Laramie Range and out of the southwest for all locations west of the Laramie Range. By 18Z Friday the NAEFS Mean Precipitable Water will increase to above the 90th percentile for portions of western Nebraska and barely into southeast Wyoming before increasing to above the 90th percentile nearly everywhere east of the Laramie Range by 00Z Saturday. Therefore, moisture will not be a limiting factor as the weak forcing moves through, as has been the case for the last several systems. The biggest concern will be whether or not the ascent from the weak shortwave and systems moving out of the southwestern CONUS will be enough to get showers going across western Nebraska. If it is, these showers are expected to remain rain with snow not anticipated at this time.

Precipitable water values will remain well over the 90th percentile for most places throughout the weekend, which may put a small damper on Halloween festivities on Saturday evening and night. This disturbances off to the southwest will push towards the region on Saturday, increasing forcing across the region. The upper-level trough over the Pacific Northwest will maintain its slow movement inland Saturday, with the trough axis sitting over Idaho and the Nevada/Utah border by early Sunday morning. A few lobes of 500mb vorticity will eject across the CWA throughout the day Saturday, but these look to be weaker than what is expected for Sunday. 700mb flow begins to amplify later Saturday into the early morning hours Sunday as the 700mb system starts to take shape across western Montana. As of now, a strong 700mb jet looks to develop just to the northeast of the CWA throughout the evening on Saturday, which would likely increase precipitation chances west of the Laramie Range as this region remains in the right entrance region of the low-level jet. Winds will also likely start picking up Saturday night into early Sunday morning for this same region. Luckily, or not if you like snow, 700mb temperatures are expected to remain well above the -2 to 0C range, likely in the 2 to 5C range, which favors any precipitation falling as rain and not snow. So what does this mean for trick-or-treating and other Halloween activities? Well, as of now, precipitation looks to hold off for the most part until early Sunday morning, unless you are trick-or-treating in the Snowy Range. Temperatures will quickly drop into the 40s for most places by 8PM Saturday night, so it looks like there will be a lot of superheroes, witches, and vampires with jackets. Luckily, precipitation should hold off until festivities end.

Much of the remainder of the long term forecast remains very uncertain as model confidence and agreement worsens Sunday through Tuesday. The early forecasting shift talked about the possibilities in depth, so please read the following for a discussion on the Sunday through Tuesday time period...

Forecast confidence decreases considerably as we head into the Sunday through Tuesday time period. While there is still potential for widespread precipitation, the ensemble spread is enormous as a very complex weather pattern sets up over the Western CONUS. First, a powerful disturbance will race into the southwest, riding on a very strong sub-tropical jet stream. Meanwhile, a northern branch trough will dive into the northwest and progress eastward simultaneously. The northern upper level low may also close off from the polar jet itself, adding to the uncertainty. With so many moving parts on the board, it is difficult to have much forecast confidence in how this will play out.

In lieu of that, we can discuss some possible scenarios. Approximately 45% of LREF members are clustered into a scenario showing a more progressive storm system. This is further split between about half of this camp showing a storm that remains progressive, and half showing a storm that eventually closes off and strengthens, but this occurs too far east to deliver much precipitation to our area. In this scenario, most of the area could expect light precipitation amounts, generally 0.25" or less. The remaining 55% of ensemble members have a deeper, stronger system with better forcing for lift, and thus improving chances for precipitation. About 30% of the full ensemble suite (a subset of the 55%) have a moderate precipitation event, where the system is strong and deep, but still progressive. The final 25% (again a subset of the 55%) depict a slow, strong upper level low closing off before reaching our area, which would lead to widespread heavy precipitation for much of the area, but especially over the High Plains. The ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index provides some additional context. EFI values for QPF on Monday are only around 0.5 to 0.7, suggesting low confidence in a significant event. However, the shift of tails values exceed 2.0 over much of the High Plains, which tells us that a small subset of ensemble members depict an extreme event. Thus, the main takeaway at this time should be that at least some light precipitation is narrowly favored (60% chance) over much of the area Sunday PM into Tuesday AM, and there is potential for significant rain and/or snow, but the probability of this scenario is fairly low (25% chance) at this time. Nonetheless, this is high enough to discuss and continue to monitor closely in the coming days. Most model guidance shows limited cold air with this system once again, and the wettest ensemble members also tend to be the warmest (as these close the low off faster). This will make snow levels an issue once again. Regardless of the precipitation outcome, expect cooler temperatures by Monday with blustery conditions. There is potential for high winds as well, but we'll wait to get a better idea of the storm's evolution before diving into those details.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As flow turns southwesterly ahead of a PacNW low, moisture begins its return to the region. The first signs of this pattern shift are expected on Friday as isolated storms will begin to pop up, though at this point QPF should be on the minimal side.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Monday through Thursday is expected to be mostly dry with seasonable temperatures.
- Precipitation chances increase this weekend and early next week. Details on the rain/snow amounts and river water levels are uncertain at this moment.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Near-zonal flow is established across the Intermountain West, maintaining relatively dry conditions for our CWA. This keeps precipitation chances near-zero for most locations with little more than scattered cloud cover expected. We're sitting near- normal in terms of high temperatures as well, leaving valleys in the 50's to low-60's, and mountain locations in the 40's to low-50's. Though we continue to dry out steadily the next few days, some valley locations may still experience fog around sunrise which may impact morning commutes.
NEXT ROUND OF PRECIPITATION THIS WEEKEND:

As flow turns southwesterly ahead of a PacNW low, moisture begins its return to the region. The first signs of this pattern shift are expected on Friday as isolated storms will begin to pop up, though at this point QPF should be on the minimal side. By Sunday though, moisture will be hitting its peak in our CWA. As guidance stands there is little confidence in the exact trajectory of the broad moisture plume. If we are to lean one way or another, more evidence is suggesting that the strongest portion of the plume will pass to our south, though even in this scenario, southwestern Colorado is in line for yet another wet stretch with PWAT's up to 300% of normal. Adding to the complexity of this event is the progression of the upper-level pattern. As the PacNW low propagates eastwards towards the northern Rockies, a second low develops at the base of the trough, swinging through the southwestern US before eventually rejoining the parent trough early in the work week. The movement of both lows would likely have significant impacts on the nature of this storm system as temperatures will plummet to around 10 degrees below normal with their passage. This could be enough to drop snow level 1-2 kft. The complex pattern continues to lead to low confidence in the timing and location of any eventual snowfall though, and as such we cannot yet speculate on how impacts will manifest from said snowfall. What we can say now though is that any notable amount of precipitation over southwestern Colorado locations recovering from last week's rainfall will have the potential to exacerbate flooding concerns. We are keeping a very close eye on this next round of precipitation as a result, and over the coming days as more details come into view we will begin to better gauge the risks Sunday into Monday morning. As such, stay tuned for additional information throughout this week.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Either way, the deepening trough out west will likely bring accumulating snow to the mountains this weekend. Showers will start more isolated in nature, increasing in coverage later in the weekend and into early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier and warmer through most of the week, with a pattern shift starting on Friday.
- Cooler and more active weather expected this weekend and into next week. Details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Weather will remain quiet across our region today. Temperatures will remain several degrees above normal, with highs in the 60s-70s over the plains, and in the high-50s for the valleys. Winds will be somewhat breezy and out of the west. Overall, a warm and quiet fall day.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Calm and mild conditions will continue on Thursday, though temperatures will drop a few degrees thanks to a dry cold front passing through.

Starting on Friday, our next incoming source of moisture will be a deepening trough over the Pacific northwest. As we move into this weekend, southwest flow aloft will increase over the region, bringing in moist Pacific air and better forcing to western Colorado. Meanwhile, deterministic guidance suggests a shortwave passing south of our area during the day on Friday, which could potentially bring some rain to the far southeast plains as well. However, if the wave picks up in speed, most of the precipitation could miss us, falling in Kansas instead.

Either way, the deepening trough out west will likely bring accumulating snow to the mountains this weekend. Showers will start more isolated in nature, increasing in coverage later in the weekend and into early next week. Latest guidance shows the upper trough amplifying, with a secondary low potentially moving onshore from the southwest as the trough digs into the Four Corners. Details on the timing, strength, and path of the system still need to be refined in the data, but overall cooler and more active weather is currently expected for next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Precipitation looks to mostly wind down Monday morning, leaving a cool northerly flow in place over the area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally dry and seasonable conditions will persist through Thursday, with a weak grazing system tonight bringing light precipitation to northern Utah and southwest Wyoming.

- Moisture will increase over the area beginning Friday, bringing an increasing threat of flash flooding. The area will see a more substantial increase in moisture and instability and thus the potential for flooding Sunday into Monday as a strong Pacific storm crosses the area.
- Much cooler temperatures will accompany the system for early next week, allowing snow levels to potentially drop as low as 7500 feet by Monday morning.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A weakening shortwave trough is currently swinging across northern Nevada and will cross far northern Utah tonight. Much like last night, this fast-moving wave will push a reinforcing cold front into northern Utah, bringing valley rain showers and light mountain snow once again. Precipitation is already ongoing near remnants of the existing boundary and will continue through late tonight. The boundary and associated precipitation is expected to remain north of around Utah County. Expect precipitation to wind down well before sunrise.

Fairly benign weather is expected on Wednesday and Thursday under a southwesterly flow aloft. Temperatures should cool slightly from today across northern Utah owing the the cold front, then rebound for Thursday. Models do depict yet another weakening trailing shortwave disturbance crossing Utah late Wednesday afternoon into Wednesday evening. The dynamics associated with that looks to be very insignificant, so very little if any precipitation is expected.

Main focus continues to be the storm system for the end of the week through the weekend. A low pressure system will slowly make its way to the PacNW coast on Thursday. On Friday, a subtle disturbance rounding the base of this low and lifting across Utah will start to spread some moisture into the area. However, with weak dynamics, expect mainly isolated to scattered showers and a few thunderstorms to develop. Main focus for heavier precipitation will be southwest Utah, otherwise amounts are expected to remain relatively light elsewhere. The 25th percentile of the NBM has no measurable precipitation for the vast majority of the forecast area and only a few hundredths of an inch in portions of southwest Utah. However, the 75th percentile has between 0.5-1 inch over portions of southwest Utah, so cannot rule out some heavier showers and isolated potential for flash flooding. On Saturday, the storm system will begin to move inland. This will maintain unsettled weather over the area, but with the better large-scale dynamics still upstream, expect generally isolated to scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms once again.

The storm system is expected to cross Utah on Sunday, although there is still some uncertainty regarding how deep it will carve into the area. This storm will also phase with a southern stream system that will be associated with an atmospheric river. The moisture plume will punch inland across far southern California and northern Baja. Some of this moisture will make it into Utah, with IVT anomalies in the 97th-99th percentile of climatology. However, there is still enough model spread regarding how much precipitation will develop over Utah. While the spread has decreased from what models were showing 24 hours ago, we are still looking at NBM 25th-75th percentile differences of 1-2 inches in areas favored in southwest flow and 0.5-1 inch elsewhere. Regardless, Sunday is expected to see the heaviest precipitation of this storm cycle, with the potential for widespread and moderate to heavy precipitation with an increased flash flood threat.

A cold front will also push into Utah on Sunday, bringing lowering snow levels. Snow amounts will be dependent on the strength of the trough and precipitation amounts, of which, as mentioned, there is still significant uncertainty. However, a general 3-6 inches with locally 10 inches or more in higher elevation sites such as near Brian Head, in the Tushars, the upper Cottonwoods, and high Uintas seem reasonable at this time.

Precipitation looks to mostly wind down Monday morning, leaving a cool northerly flow in place over the area. Models then start to diverge on the large-scale pattern, with how quickly the storm continues to progress east out of the area and whether a strong ridge builds into the area behind it or whether another storm system manages to move into the area midweek.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')
